claims.text: The alloy is a multiphase eutectic AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with interpenetrating lamellar or honeycomb phases.
All phases initially possess intact protective oxide scales.
Wear preferentially removes the protective oxide at phase boundaries.
Oxide removal exposes fresh surfaces belonging to phases with different electrochemical potentials.
The exposed phase interfaces form localized galvanic cells.
Localized galvanic coupling accelerates corrosion at the exposed interfaces.
Galvanically accelerated corrosion further reduces the alloy's resistance to wear.
The reciprocal interaction between oxide removal, galvanic corrosion, and reduced wear resistance creates a degradation feedback loop.
Combined wear-corrosion produces greater total degradation than either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Combined exposure produces deeper wear tracks than the isolated-condition baseline.
Combined exposure produces more extensive and frequent corrosion pits than the isolated-condition baseline.
Both the wear rate and the corrosion rate increase during simultaneous exposure because of wear-corrosion synergy.
In isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests, the protective oxide partially remains intact.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 300 °C in a chloride-containing aqueous environment under cyclic sliding.
Substantial changes in temperature or chloride concentration may alter oxide stability or galvanic interactions and diminish the mechanism's validity.
Applied load, sliding frequency, and local microstructural heterogeneity may change the quantitative contributions of oxide removal and galvanic corrosion.
Nominally identical samples should be compared under combined tribocorrosion, wear-only, and corrosion-only conditions.
Localized potential mapping and oxide-scale analysis can be used to test whether oxide removal and localized galvanic activity accompany degradation.

contradictions.description: The baseline attributes retained oxide in both isolated tests to the absence of simultaneous mechanical disruption, but the wear-only arm explicitly includes sliding and the mechanism states that wear mechanically strips the oxide. Partial oxide retention is possible, but the stated rationale for it is internally inconsistent for the wear-only condition.

The prediction requires combined degradation to exceed either isolated response, whereas the falsification rule uses the stronger benchmark of exceeding the sum of the isolated effects. These are different definitions of accelerated or synergistic degradation.
